evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in health systems of the WHO European region: implementation, applications, opportunities, and barriers
evidence.outcome: Stakeholder groups engaged by Member States on AI, including patients and the public
evidence.effect: Of 36 Member States reporting engagement, patient associations were engaged by 42% (15/36) and the general public by 22% (8/36). Government actors (81%), providers (75%), and developers (75%) were engaged more often.
evidence.quote: Of the 36 Member States reporting at least one form of engagement, the stakeholders most frequently engaged were government actors (81%; 29/36), healthcare providers (75%; 27/36), and AI developers (75%; 27/36), whereas patient associations (42%; 15/36) and the general public (22%; 8/36) were less commonly involved.
evidence.country: WHO European Region (50 of 53 Member States)

commentary.bottom_line: Forty-six sources endorse continuous multidisciplinary and patient engagement across the AI lifecycle, but no supplied study tests whether such engagement identifies emerging risks or prevents harm. One descriptive survey of WHO European Member States found that patients and the public were engaged less often than government, providers, and developers.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests whether continuous stakeholder engagement detects new risks or improves outcomes. The single study is a descriptive survey of 50 WHO European Member States. It documents who is engaged, not what engagement achieves. The endorsements are mostly commentaries, so the support rests on expert opinion rather than tests of the practice.

Of 36 Member States that reported engagement, 15 (42%) engaged patient associations and 8 (22%) engaged the general public. By comparison, 81% engaged government actors and 75% engaged providers and developers. These figures suggest that patient and public voices may be the groups most often absent from national AI engagement.

The survey did not report whether marginalized, low-income, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups took part. Several endorsing commentaries call for community champions and representatives of marginalised groups. No supplied study examines whether engaging these groups changes AI design, deployment decisions, or outcomes for them.

The endorsements include a consensus guideline (FUTURE-AI), an industry assurance guide (CHAI), and NIST AI 600-1. The NIST passage quoted here addresses risk tolerance and model decommissioning rather than stakeholder engagement. None of the supplied sources describes a binding legal requirement to engage patients or communities.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI deployments with and without structured, ongoing stakeholder engagement. Future work should measure the number and timing of risks identified after initial design, downstream patient harms, and the staff time and cost of engagement. It should also report which formats of patient and community representation were used and which populations the representatives came from.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The one hazard survey reports national-level engagement in European countries and does not describe these groups. Its relevance to U.S. safety-net settings is therefore uncertain, and health systems serving these populations have no evidence on which engagement approaches reach them.
